name: Text to SQL Benchmarks
title: Text to SQL Benchmarks
answer: Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD score text to SQL systems by running the generated query and comparing its result with a known correct answer. They measure execution accuracy and, in some cases, exact set match on held out questions across multiple database schemas. Enterprise schemas are larger and less tidy than the benchmarks, so real accuracy is usually lower. The scope also includes multilingual questions and complex SQL features such as nested queries and window functions.

sections.body: Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD score text to SQL systems by running the generated query and comparing its result with a known correct answer. They measure execution accuracy and, in some cases, exact set match on held out questions across multiple database schemas. Enterprise schemas are larger and less tidy than the benchmarks, so real accuracy is usually lower. The scope also includes multilingual questions and complex SQL features such as nested queries and window functions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Benchmark evaluation typically runs on local or containerized database instances, often SQLite for small schemas and PostgreSQL for larger ones. The harness parses the generated SQL, executes it against the reference database, and compares the returned rows with the expected result. Leaderboard runs may use isolated compute to prevent interference between submissions.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Datasets are split into training, development, and test sets, with each question paired to a reference SQL query. Systems receive the natural language question and the database schema, then generate a query through schema linking, few shot prompting, or fine tuning. Scoring uses execution accuracy, exact set match, and sometimes a valid efficiency score that rewards shorter runtimes for correct results.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Benchmark datasets carry academic or open licenses, and their schemas and questions have specific provenance that users should check before commercial use. A known risk is test set contamination, where models trained on benchmark questions or queries report inflated scores. Some datasets include synthetic or anonymized data to reduce privacy exposure, but real enterprise data is rarely shared in public benchmarks.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Future benchmarks are moving toward larger, messier enterprise style schemas and private evaluation sets that resist contamination. Multi turn questions, ambiguous requests, and agentic workflows that plan and revise SQL are becoming part of the evaluation. Metrics are also expanding to include cost, latency, and whether the system asks for clarification instead of guessing.
